newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: European chemical firms urge stronger patent laws.
newsitem.headline: European chemical firms urge stronger patent laws.

text.p: Representatives of European chemical firms called on Wednesday for an effective continent-wide system of patent laws to help stop investment draining away to the United States and Japan.

Leaders of the European Chemical Industry Council (CEFIC) also urged action to ensure global intellectual property rules were enshrined in national laws, especially in countries seen weak on patent protection like India and Argentina.

"Our fundamental requirement as a research-intensive global industry is clear: we need effective patent laws that apply internationally to the greatest extent possible," CEFIC president Jurgen Dormann told a news conference.

Daniel Wagniere of the Swiss-based pharmaceutical giant Novartis said although the chemical industry remained a mainstay of the continental economy, the United States and Japan had recently begun to attract more investment.
"The capital spending figures reflect poorer returns on capital, economic uncertainty and greater legislative impediments in Europe, particularly when compared with the U.S.," he added.

Dormann, Chairman of the Board of Germany's Hoechst, and Wagniere said an effective and updated framework for patent registration and protection could help halt the trend and make European firms more competitive again.
At present, new registrations have to go through the Munich-based European Patent Office and are then applied only in the countries nominated by the patent holder.
Costs of obtaining a patent are up to 10 times those in the United States, said Brian Yorke, head of corporate intellectual property at Novartis.

But the industry representatives said a European Union accord, the Community Patent Convention initiated in 1975 but yet to go into force, would increase costs through a requirement for translations into all 15 EU languages.

Yorke said it would also provide weaker protection since if a local court in any EU country found a patent approved under the convention was against national law it would be invalidated, pending appeal, across the Union.

The CEFIC officials were speaking during a conference on patents marking their Brussels-based organisation's 25th anniversary and held at the headquarters of the United Nations' World Intellectual Property Organisation (WIPO).

They hailed the 1993 global agreement on trade in intellectual property, or TRIPS, one of the underlying accords of the World Trade Organisation (WTO), as marking strong progress towards a single international patent system.
But, said Dormann, "TRIPS must now be further developed and effectively translated into national legislation, particularly in countries with weak patent laws."

Yorke said several emerging Asian "tiger" economies, as well as China, had strong patent protection laws -- although in China there remained a question mark on enforcement or "what might happen when you get into the courts".
But India and Argentina -- where the TRIPS accord has been the subject of fierce political debate -- were weak and had "large imitative industries with their own interests at stake".
